blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Medical segmentation uncertainty is often evaluated with calibration error or pixel-level error-detection scores, but these metrics do not show whether uncertainty improves downstream review decisions. We propose a decision-aware evaluation protocol that separates uncertainty estimation from deferral policy and evaluates their combination under fixed review budgets: which pixels, regions, or images should be accepted, and which should be reviewed. The protocol reports fixed-budget error reduction, risk-coverage behaviour, region-level review proxies, structural failure modes, probability-derived baselines, and sensitivity to review assumptions. We instantiate it across retinal vessel, skin lesion, and polyp segmentation with multiple backbones and uncertainty estimators. Under matched inference budgets and canonical multi-layer MC Dropout, test-time augmentation (TTA) gives a stronger error-detection signal across matched MC--TTA comparisons, including architecture and dropout-placement checks. However, estimator rankings are not universal. For example, probability-derived scores remain competitive, deep ensembles can outperform TTA, learned deferral helps mainly when the base estimator is weak, and rankings can change with review unit, uncertainty target, correction assumptions, and cost model. Structural and second-observer analyses further show that boundary and thin-structure failures are partly tied to annotation ambiguity. These findings support evaluating uncertainty as an estimator-policy-review configuration, not as a standalone score map. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Uncertainity-in-Medical-Image-Segmentation/README.md

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
A medical segmentation model is rarely the final actor in a clinical or
annotation workflow. Its mask is inspected, corrected, accepted, or escalated.
What matters is therefore not only whether the model is accurate on average, but
whether it can indicate when its output should not be trusted. This distinction
is easy to miss. A model may report a high Dice score while failing on the cases
that make review necessary: ambiguous boundaries, thin vessels, small polyps, or
images with artefacts. In such settings, uncertainty is valuable only if it
changes the downstream decision of which pixels, regions, or images should be
accepted and which should be reviewed under a limited budget.

blocks.en:
Most work on uncertainty in medical segmentation evaluates the uncertainty map as
an object in itself. Calibration error, predictive likelihood, and pixel-level
error-detection AUROC [ 12 , 24 , 28 ] ask whether uncertainty values are numerically meaningful or whether they rank
mistakes well. These are important questions, but they are not the whole
deployment question. Two uncertainty scores with similar AUROC can select
different pixels at a 10% review budget. A better calibrated model can still
leave more residual error after deferral. A segmentation model without an
explicit review rule has no operating point: it has a score map, but not a
decision.

blocks.en:
This paper argues that segmentation uncertainty should be evaluated at the point
where it is used. We separate estimation , the procedure that produces an
uncertainty or confidence field, from decision , the policy that converts
that field into accept/defer choices. This separation turns uncertainty
evaluation into a practical question: under the same review budget, which
estimator and policy remove more error, retain safer predictions, and expose the
failure modes that would otherwise remain hidden? It also changes what counts as
a fair baseline. In binary segmentation, common probability-derived scores such
as entropy, margin, inverse confidence, and distance from 1 / 2 1/2 collapse to the
same ranking. These free scores should therefore be treated as first-class
comparators, not as weak baselines.

blocks.en:
We propose a decision-aware evaluation protocol for medical image segmentation.
The protocol pairs uncertainty estimators with deferral policies and reports
fixed-budget error reduction, risk–coverage behaviour, region-level review
proxies, structural stratification, probability-derived baselines, and
sensitivity to review assumptions under the same decision rule. It is an
evaluation practice rather than a new architecture or reject rule: any backbone,
uncertainty estimator, or review policy can be inserted, but all are judged by
the decisions they enable under explicit review budgets.

blocks.en:
We instantiate the protocol across retinal vessel, skin lesion, and polyp
segmentation with multiple backbones and uncertainty estimators. The results show
that estimator rankings are decision-dependent. Under matched inference budgets
and canonical multi-layer MC Dropout, test-time augmentation (TTA) gives a
stronger error-detection signal across matched MC–TTA comparisons, including
complementary-architecture and dropout-placement checks. However, TTA is not a
universal winner: probability-derived scores remain competitive, deep ensembles
can outperform TTA on some datasets, and learned deferral heads help mainly when
the base estimator is weak. Review assumptions also matter: rankings can change
with the review unit, uncertainty target, correction model, and cost function.
Structural and second-observer analyses further show that boundary and
thin-structure failures are partly tied to annotation ambiguity, but are not
explained away by it.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Medical segmentation models and foundation models. Medical segmentation has progressed from U-Net-style CNNs [ 36 , 46 ] to self-configuring pipelines [ 19 ] , transformer hybrids [ 6 ] , vision-language foundation models [ 25 , 16 , 45 ] and
promptable foundation models [ 23 , 26 , 35 , 15 ] , whose zero-shot medical
use has been benchmarked across modalities [ 27 ] . These
works ask how to build or adapt stronger segmenters. Our question is
orthogonal: given a trained segmenter, how should its uncertainty be evaluated
when it drives review decisions? We therefore hold the backbone fixed within
each dataset–backbone cell when comparing estimators and policies, and include
complementary architecture checks to test whether the observed decision patterns
are tied to one backbone family. A SAM/MedSAM extension treats the prompt as an
additional decision variable, but keeps promptable models outside the controlled
trained-backbone matrix.

blocks.en: 3 Decision-Aware Evaluation Protocol
blocks.zh: 3 知情评估议定书

blocks.en:
We evaluate segmentation uncertainty as part of a review decision, not as a
standalone map. The protocol has two stages ( Fig. 1 ). First, an estimator takes an image and a trained segmentation backbone and returns
a probability map p ^ \hat{p} , a hard prediction y ^ \hat{y} , and an uncertainty or
score map u u . Second, a deferral policy ranks review units such as
pixels, patches, connected components, or images, and at budget β \beta accepts
the 1 − β 1-\beta fraction with the lowest review score while deferring the rest.
Thus, the protocol separates how uncertainty is estimated from how it is used.

blocks.en: 3.1 Uncertainty estimators and score maps
blocks.zh: 3.1 不确定估计和计分图

blocks.en:
Within each dataset–backbone cell, the segmentation backbone is held fixed when
comparing estimators and policies. MC Dropout [ 12 ] keeps dropout active at test time, freezes normalization
layers, averages stochastic forward passes, and reports predictive variance or
mutual information. Our primary MC–TTA comparison uses canonical multi-layer MC
Dropout under matched inference budgets; dropout placement, dropout rate,
stochastic realization, and training seed are audited separately. TTA [ 3 ] averages label-preserving geometric transforms after
inverse warping and uses variation across transformed predictions as
uncertainty. We evaluate matched TTA subsets and the full six-transform set.

blocks.en:
We report results as decision-level findings. Under matched-budget controls,
TTA gives a stronger error-detection signal than canonical MC Dropout, but the
broader evaluation shows that estimator rankings are not universal. Rankings
change with estimator family, review unit, uncertainty target, correction
assumption, and cost model. The main result is therefore not a single winning
uncertainty method, but the need to evaluate uncertainty as an
estimator–policy–review configuration.

blocks.en: 6 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en:
The results support a simple conclusion: segmentation uncertainty should be
evaluated by the review decisions it enables, not by the score map alone. Under
matched budgets and canonical multi-layer MC Dropout, TTA gives a stronger
error-ranking signal across our MC–TTA comparisons. However, the broader
benchmark does not support a universal estimator ranking: deep ensembles can
outperform TTA on some datasets, probability-derived scores remain competitive,
learned deferral is not uniformly better than raw uncertainty, and review
assumptions can change the preferred method. These patterns would be obscured by
reporting only calibration error or a single pooled Unc-AUROC.

alternative softmax-derived scores do not necessarily imply better review
decisions.

all segmentation tasks. We therefore treat cross-dataset counts as
benchmark evidence rather than universal claims.

blocks.en: 8 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 8 结论

blocks.en:
We presented a decision-aware evaluation protocol for medical segmentation
uncertainty. The central claim is that uncertainty should be judged by the review
decisions it enables under explicit budgets, not by calibration or
error-detection scores alone. By separating uncertainty estimation from deferral
policy, the protocol compares MC Dropout, TTA, deep ensembles,
probability-derived scores, and learned review policies as
estimator–policy–review configurations. Within our benchmark, matched-budget
TTA gives a stronger error-ranking signal than canonical multi-layer MC Dropout,
but the broader evaluation does not support a universal estimator ordering:
deep ensembles can outperform TTA on some datasets, probability-derived scores
remain competitive, learned deferral is not uniformly better than raw
uncertainty, and review assumptions can change the preferred method. Structural
and second-observer analyses further show that boundary and thin-structure
failures are partly tied to annotation ambiguity. These findings argue against
choosing an uncertainty estimator from a single score-level metric. Instead,
uncertainty should be audited on the target distribution, at the intended review
budget, and with review units and assumptions that reflect the workflow. We will
release the protocol, code, artifacts, and summaries to support reproducible
decision-aware evaluation on new datasets, backbones, estimators, and review
policies.
